medium.titulo: Claude Code Subagents Explained by Example: Build a Test Runner Step by Step
medium.resumo: Keep long test output out of your conversation with a helper that runs in its own context and sends back only the failures
medium.conteudo_html:
Keep long test output out of your conversation with a helper that runs in its own context and sends back only the failures

Have you noticed your Claude Code conversation filling up with long test results, logs and search output?

Subagents keep it clean. A subagent is a helper that does a noisy job in its own space and sends back only a short summary.

In this article you’ll learn what a subagent is, when to use one, and then we’ll build a real one together, step by step: a test runner that runs your tests and reports only the failures.

🎥 Prefer video? Watch the full tutorial here:

https://medium.com/media/d23929111a86ba90c40bf41afdac5b41/href

What is a subagent?

A subagent is a specialized helper that Claude can hand a task to, like a teammate you delegate a job to.

  • It works in its own context window (its own working memory), with its own instructions and only the tools you allow.
  • When it’s done, it sends back only a short summary to your main conversation.
  • It’s just a Markdown file, with a short header and instructions.

How a subagent works

  1. Claude delegates. When your request matches a subagent’s description, Claude hands the task over.
  2. The subagent works alone, with a fresh context, its own instructions, and only the tools you gave it.
  3. Only a summary comes back. All the long output stays inside the subagent.

So your main conversation stays clean, and focused on your real work.

Four reasons to use subagents

  1. Save context. Noisy output, like logs and test results, stays out of your conversation.
  2. Limit tools. For example, a test runner that can run commands but can’t edit your files.
  3. Specialize. Each subagent gets focused instructions for one job.
  4. Lower costs. You can send simple jobs to a faster, cheaper model, like Haiku.

When to use one

Stay in the main conversation for back-and-forth work, quick changes, and steps that share a lot of context.

Use a subagent when a task:

  • produces lots of output you won’t need again,
  • needs strict limits on tools,
  • or can simply end with a summary.

Our example: a test runner

Running a test suite prints a lot: here, 68 lines, and all of it lands in your conversation. A test-runner subagent runs the tests in its own context and sends back just the failures, and where to look.

The problem without a subagent

Here’s a small shop project: a cart file and 30 tests. I start Claude Code and ask it to run the tests.

Claude runs them right in the main conversation, so every line of the output goes into its context window. One failure, but all 68 lines now take up space in Claude’s working memory. Do this a few times, and your session fills up with noise.

Step 1: Create the file

Subagents for a project live in .claude/agents, one Markdown file per subagent:

mkdir -p .claude/agents

Then create .claude/agents/test-runner.md.

  • .claude/agents/: this project, shared via git.
  • ~/.claude/agents/: all your projects.

Step 2: Write the header

Like a skill, a subagent starts with a short header between two lines of dashes:

---
name: test-runner
description: Runs the project's tests and reports only the failures. Use proactively after code changes, or when the user asks to run the tests.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: haiku
---
  • name is how you and Claude refer to it.
  • description is the key line: Claude reads it to decide when to delegate. “Use proactively” tells Claude it can call this helper on its own.
  • tools is an allow list: Read, Grep, Glob and Bash. No Edit or Write, so this helper can run tests but can never change your code.
  • model: haiku sends this simple job to a faster, cheaper model. Write inherit to use the same model as your conversation.

Step 3: Write the instructions

Everything below the header becomes the subagent’s own system prompt:

You run tests and report the results. You never edit files.
 
When invoked:
1. Run the test suite: python -m pytest -q
2. If every test passes, reply in one line with the number of passed tests.
3. For each failing test, report:
   - the test name
   - the error: expected value vs. actual value
   - the file and line most likely causing it
4. Keep the report under 15 lines. Never paste the full test output.

The most important rule is the last one: keep it short and never paste the full output. That’s what keeps your conversation clean.

Step 4: Test it

Because the agents folder is brand new, start a fresh Claude Code session so it picks it up. Then make the same request: "Run the tests".

This time, Claude delegates: you see a line with the subagent’s name, test-runner, and a short task description. Here's everything that comes back: one failure, what was expected, and exactly where to look. No wall of output.

It even found the cause: the code says total > 100, but the rule is "100 or more", so an order of exactly 100 gets no discount.

I ask Claude to fix it. Because the description says “use proactively”, Claude runs the test runner again to check the fix.

You can also call it yourself. Type @, pick the agent, and that subagent is guaranteed to run:

@agent-test-runner check everything still passes

Step 5: Go further (4 tips)

  1. Keep the description short and clear. Say what it does and when to use it. Descriptions load into every session, so short is better.
  2. Give it only the tools it needs. Testers and reviewers usually don’t need Edit or Write.
  3. Pick the right model. haiku for simple jobs, inherit when the task needs your main model.
  4. Share it. Commit the .claude/agents folder to git, and your whole team gets the same helpers.

Recap

  • A subagent is a helper with its own context, its own instructions and its own tools.
  • You create it with one Markdown file in the agents folder: a name, a description, tools and a model.
  • Use it for noisy, self-contained tasks, so only the summary comes back.

Get the files

The subagent file and the demo project (30 tests, one real bug) are free on GitHub:

👉 Files: https://github.com/NEDBS12/youtube-tuto/tree/main/claude-code-subagents

🎥 Watch the video tutorial: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SVyg2gwWEd4

medium.titulo: Every Page of Your SPA Deserves a Preview: SEO for Vue and React Without Nuxt or Next.js
medium.resumo: Every Page of Your SPA Deserves a Preview: SEO for Vue and React Without Nuxt or Next.js
medium.conteudo_html:
Every Page of Your SPA Deserves a Preview: SEO for Vue and React Without Nuxt or Next.js

You share a product page on WhatsApp. Instead of the product image and name, the preview displays your website’s generic title. Sometimes, nothing appears at all. You try sharing another link from the same website and get the same result.

Google is not much better. Your pages appear with identical titles and descriptions, even though each page contains different content.

If you build applications with Vue or React, you have probably encountered this problem. Your application works perfectly in the browser, but search engines and social media platforms struggle to understand what each page is about.

I spent four years looking for a practical solution to this problem. Eventually, I built one.

Why This Happens

Most Vue and React single-page applications (SPAs) follow the same approach. The server sends a basic HTML document, and JavaScript renders the actual content in the browser.

Consider a typical HTML response:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <title>My Application</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Welcome to my application">
</head>
<body>
  <div id="app"></div>
  <script src="/assets/app.js"></script>
</body>
</html>

The browser loads the JavaScript bundle, and Vue or React renders the appropriate page. When users navigate to different routes, the application updates the content without requesting an entirely new HTML document.

This is excellent for building interactive applications. However, it creates a problem for social media crawlers and can complicate search engine optimization.

When someone shares a product URL on WhatsApp, Facebook, LinkedIn, or another platform, the platform’s crawler typically requests the URL and inspects the HTML response. It looks for metadata such as the page title, description, preview image, and canonical URL.

If every route returns the same HTML metadata, every shared link can produce the same preview.

Search engines can execute JavaScript in some circumstances, but relying on client-side rendering alone does not provide the same level of control as delivering the appropriate metadata in the initial HTML response.

Four Years of Searching for a Solution

For years, the usual recommendations have been Nuxt for Vue or Next.js for React. Both frameworks offer powerful server-side rendering (SSR) and static site generation (SSG) capabilities.

But what if your application is already built with Vue or React? What if your backend is already running on Laravel, Express, or another framework? What if you simply want each page to have the correct metadata without rebuilding your entire application?

Migrating to another framework is not always a realistic option.

Sometimes, you need a smaller, more targeted solution that fits into your existing architecture.

[Add one or two sentences describing the project where you first encountered this problem.]

I wanted a solution that would work with an existing SPA, generate page-specific metadata on the server, and leave the application’s frontend architecture untouched.

The Breakthrough: You Only Need the <head>

The key insight was simple: you do not necessarily need to render the entire page on the server to deliver the correct metadata.

For social media previews and many metadata-related SEO requirements, the important part is the HTML <head> section.

For example, a product page could return the following metadata:

<head>
  <title>Wireless Headphones | My Store</title>
  <meta
    name="description"
    content="Discover our wireless headphones with premium sound."
  >
  <meta
    property="og:title"
    content="Wireless Headphones | My Store"
  >
  <meta
    property="og:description"
    content="Discover our wireless headphones with premium sound."
  >
  <meta
    property="og:image"
    content="https://example.com/images/headphones.jpg"
  >
  <meta
    property="og:url"
    content="https://example.com/products/wireless-headphones"
  >
  <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
</head>

The browser can still load the SPA and render the page as usual. The difference is that crawlers receive the correct metadata directly in the HTML response.

This approach does not replace full SSR or SSG. It addresses a more specific problem: delivering page-specific metadata without requiring a complete rendering framework.

Meet spa-meta-tags

I built spa-meta-tags, an open-source package designed to inject dynamic metadata into the HTML responses of existing single-page applications.

The idea is to keep your current architecture while making your pages more suitable for search engines and social media previews.

Installation

npm install spa-meta-tags

Basic example with Express

The package can be integrated into an existing Express server. You provide the metadata for the requested page, and the middleware injects it into your HTML response.

A simplified integration looks like this:

const express = require('express');
const { SpaMetaTags } = require('spa-meta-tags');
const app = express();
const spaMetaTags = new SpaMetaTags({
  // Configure the package according to your application.
});
// Register the metadata middleware before the SPA fallback.
app.use(async (req, res, next) => {
  try {
    // Resolve metadata for the requested URL.
    // Apply it to the HTML response using spa-meta-tags.
    next();
  } catch (error) {
    next(error);
  }
});
// Serve your SPA's static files and fallback route here.

Consult the official documentation for the exact configuration options and complete working examples.

The important architectural principle is that the metadata must be resolved for the requested URL before the HTML response is sent. Your SPA can then continue operating as before.

What Changes for SEO?

With page-specific metadata delivered in the initial HTML response, you can provide different information for different routes.

1. Unique titles and descriptions

Each product, article, category, or landing page can have its own title and description.

This helps search engines understand the purpose of each page and gives users more relevant information in search results when that metadata is used.

2. Better social media previews

Open Graph metadata allows supported platforms to display the appropriate title, description, and image when a link is shared.

Instead of showing the same generic preview for every URL, your application can provide information that matches the actual page.

3. Canonical URLs

You can define the canonical URL for each page to indicate its preferred address to search engines.

This is useful when the same content can be accessed through multiple URLs.

4. Route-specific metadata and status handling

Different routes can return different metadata, including information appropriate for unavailable pages.

However, metadata alone does not make a nonexistent page a genuine HTTP 404 response. The server must also return the correct HTTP status code when a resource does not exist.

An important distinction

spa-meta-tags focuses on the HTML <head>. It does not automatically render the visible content of your application on the server.

If your goal is to make the entire page content available in the initial HTML response, or if you need broader SSR capabilities, Nuxt, Next.js, or another SSR/SSG solution may be more appropriate.

The purpose of spa-meta-tags is different: it provides a focused solution for metadata without forcing you to migrate your application.

Beyond SEO: Multi-Tenant Applications

While working on this solution, I also considered another use case: multi-tenant applications.

Imagine a platform where several companies have their own storefronts, subdomains, or custom domains. Each tenant needs its own metadata, branding, and potentially its own domain verification tags.

For example:

<meta
  name="facebook-domain-verification"
  content="TENANT_SPECIFIC_VERIFICATION_CODE"
>
<meta
  name="google-site-verification"
  content="TENANT_SPECIFIC_VERIFICATION_CODE"
>

These values may differ from one tenant to another.

By resolving the appropriate configuration on the server, you can return the correct metadata for the domain or tenant associated with the incoming request.

This makes the approach useful beyond traditional SEO, especially for SaaS platforms, marketplaces, and multi-tenant applications.

Beyond Metadata

[Keep this section only if script injection is available in the published version 1.1.0.]

The same principle can also be extended to scripts that need to be present in the initial HTML response.

For example, some applications need to configure analytics or tracking tools such as Google Tag Manager, Facebook Pixel, or TikTok Pixel.

In a multi-tenant platform, the configuration may differ between tenants. Handling this at the server level can help ensure that the appropriate configuration is included in the HTML response.

Check the published package version and documentation before including this capability in the article.

Technical Decisions Behind the Package

Building a small package that fits into existing applications requires careful decisions. Here are some of the principles behind the project.

Zero dependencies

Keeping the dependency footprint small reduces installation overhead and avoids introducing unnecessary packages into an existing application.

Flexible integration

The goal is to integrate with an existing server rather than force developers to replace their frontend framework or rewrite their application.

Graceful failure

Metadata generation should not become a reason for an application to stop responding. When an external API or metadata source is unavailable, the server should be able to fall back to a safe response.

The package’s exact timeout and fallback behavior should be verified against the published version before documenting specific limits.

Safe HTML injection

Metadata values must be handled carefully before being inserted into HTML. Escaping values appropriately helps prevent malformed markup and injection vulnerabilities.

Caching

When metadata is expensive to retrieve or generate, caching can reduce repeated work. The caching strategy must account for differences between routes and tenants to avoid returning one page’s metadata for another.

Support for different deployment environments

Not every application runs on a dedicated Node.js server. Some projects are deployed to platforms such as Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, or GitHub Pages, while others use traditional shared hosting.

The appropriate implementation depends on the deployment environment. A server-side middleware solution requires a server or compatible runtime. Static hosting generally needs metadata to be generated during the build process or handled through another supported mechanism.

Check the documentation for the deployment modes actually supported by spa-meta-tags.

How to Get Started

If you already have a Vue or React SPA and want to improve its page metadata without migrating to Nuxt or Next.js, start by exploring the project.

  • Documentation: roazagba.github.io/spa-meta-tags
  • GitHub repository: github.com/roazagba/spa-meta-tags
  • npm package: npmjs.com/package/spa-meta-tags

Review the installation instructions and examples to determine whether the package fits your current architecture.

Final Thoughts

Single-page applications offer a great developer experience, but page-specific metadata can become a challenge when the initial HTML response is identical across routes.

Nuxt and Next.js provide comprehensive solutions through SSR and SSG. However, migrating an existing application is not always necessary or practical when the immediate requirement is to deliver the correct metadata.

That is the problem spa-meta-tags aims to solve.

The broader lesson is that you do not always need to replace your entire architecture to address a specific technical limitation. Sometimes, a small, carefully designed addition is enough to make an existing application work better.

If you build Vue or React applications, I would be interested to hear how you currently handle SEO and social media previews in your projects.

medium.titulo: Microfrontends Are Easier Than You Think
medium.resumo: Can React, Vue, and Angular live together in one application?
medium.conteudo_html:
Can React, Vue, and Angular live together in one application?

I have several years of experience working with microfrontends. In one of my previous projects, we had 20+ microfrontends.

That experience gave me a practical understanding of the architectural challenges that arise as applications grow, teams expand, and deployment processes become more complex.

Recently, I built a small microfrontend application to explore how different frontend frameworks can coexist in the same application.

The host application is built with React, and it loads independent microfrontends built with:

⚛️ React · 🟢 Vue · 🅰️ Angular

I used Module Federation to load the applications independently.

You can see my example here: 🔗 https://github.com/maximkaby/module-federation-react-vue-angular-example

But making them work together is only the beginning. The more interesting questions are: How do you manage routing? How do microfrontends communicate? And is this architecture actually worth the complexity?

🛣️ Routing

One approach is to let the host application own the main routing, while each microfrontend manages its internal routes.

For example:

  • / → React host application
  • /products/* → React microfrontend
  • /analytics/* → Vue microfrontend
  • /settings/* → Angular microfrontend

The host determines which microfrontend to load, while each microfrontend handles navigation within its own area.

This creates clear ownership and allows teams to develop their parts independently.

✅ Pros

Independent development

Different teams can work on separate applications without constantly changing the same codebase.

Independent deployments

This is one of the biggest advantages for large applications.

When everything is tightly coupled to a single build and release process, deployments can become a bottleneck. Unrelated changes may delay releases, consume unnecessary build resources, increase costs, and introduce risks caused by changes elsewhere in the codebase.

With well-designed microfrontends, teams can build, test, and deploy their applications independently, reducing coordination overhead and making releases more predictable.

Technology freedom

Different parts of a product can use different frameworks when there is a good reason to do so. React, Vue, and Angular can coexist within the same overall application.

Incremental migration of legacy applications

One interesting use case for Module Federation is modernizing applications with a large amount of legacy code.

Imagine you have a large application running on an old version of React. Upgrading the entire codebase can be risky, time-consuming, and expensive.

With Module Federation, you can introduce a new microfrontend using a newer React version without migrating the entire application at once.

This allows you to modernize the product incrementally, reduce the scope of risky changes, and avoid a large-scale rewrite.

Of course, different React versions require careful dependency configuration and isolation to avoid runtime conflicts.

⚠️ Things to Consider Before Adopting Microfrontends

Communication becomes harder

Sharing state and coordinating events between microfrontends isn’t as straightforward as communication within a single application. Clear contracts and explicit communication patterns are essential.

Documentation and architecture decisions

As the number of microfrontends grows, clear documentation becomes essential.

Document shared modules, integration contracts, routing rules, proxy configuration, and deployment processes. Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) help explain why particular architectural decisions were made and prevent teams from repeating old discussions or introducing conflicting solutions.

The goal is to make the architecture understandable not only to the current team but also to developers who join the project in the future.

Proxy configuration and CORS

Each microfrontend may run on a different local development server or origin. This can introduce CORS issues when the host application communicates with independently running applications or their APIs.

Configure development proxies where needed and define clear rules for routing requests to the appropriate service.

Remember that a development proxy doesn’t automatically solve production CORS issues. Production deployments still need an appropriate origin, reverse-proxy, or server-side CORS configuration.

UX consistency

Different teams can introduce inconsistent UI patterns unless they follow a shared design system and common frontend standards.

Finally, you only need to set these things up once. It may take 1–2 days, but it will save you a lot of time later.

🤖 Microfrontends in the AI Era

Microfrontends can accelerate development, especially in the AI era, when we’re generating and changing code faster than ever.

AI coding tools can help you integrate Module Federation into an existing project. The Module Federation Agent Skills repository provides AI agent skills to help with Module Federation implementation and integration.

🔗 https://github.com/module-federation/agent-skills

By dividing a large application into smaller, more isolated parts, we can reduce the blast radius of some bugs and make issues easier to identify and fix.

Of course, microfrontends don’t automatically prevent bugs or guarantee isolation. Good architecture, testing, monitoring, and clear boundaries are still essential.

🤔 So, Is It Worth It?

Microfrontends are a natural evolution of your project as your codebase grows, your team expands, and development speed becomes increasingly important.

You don’t need to start a project with microfrontends. Module Federation gives you the flexibility to integrate separate applications when the need arises, allowing you to evolve your architecture incrementally instead of rewriting everything from scratch.

For me, every architectural decision should solve a real problem.

In my experience, microfrontends can solve many challenges in large projects, especially when multiple teams work on parallel tasks, increasing both development speed and code quality.

The goal isn’t to adopt microfrontends just because you can. It’s to build an architecture that helps your team deliver better software, faster.

corrida_no_ar.titulo: CHOQUE no TRAIL: O exame POSITIVO de ROSÁLIA
corrida_no_ar.resumo: A atleta de trail Rosália Camargo é pega no doping na La Misión. Corredor reclama por ser impedido de competir na elite da Maratona de Pomerode, e organização esclarece. E mais: resultados da Ultra BM e a última etapa do ASICS Run Challenge.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Quarta-feira | 21 de outubro de 2026

A renomada atleta de trail run brasileira, Rosália Camargo, foi pega no exame antidoping realizado na prova La Misión deste ano. A competição, uma das maiores do país, recebeu pela primeira vez a chancela Ouro da Confederação Brasileira de Atletismo (CBAt), o que tornou obrigatória a realização de testes antidoping — uma demanda antiga da comunidade de trail.

O exame, realizado em 14 de agosto, dia em que Rosália competiu nos 25 km, detectou a presença de testosterona. A informação foi divulgada ontem pela Autoridade Brasileira de Controle de Dopagem (ABCD), que já aplicou uma suspensão provisória à atleta. Com isso, ela está impedida de participar de qualquer competição até que o caso seja julgado e uma decisão definitiva seja tomada.

Procurada pela revista “Trail Running”, Rosália, que tem 47 anos, informou que está na menopausa e faz tratamento médico. No entanto, o uso de testosterona por atletas femininas só é permitido com uma Autorização de Uso Terapêutico (AUT) emitida pela própria ABCD, o que, ao que tudo indica, não era o caso, já que a suspensão foi imediata. Geralmente, tratamentos de reposição hormonal para mulheres na menopausa utilizam outros hormônios, como progesterona e estradiol.

Atleta reclama por ser impedido de correr em Pomerode; organização responde

O atleta Renato Cirino publicou um vídeo nas redes sociais reclamando por ter sido impedido de correr na Maratona de Pomerode. Segundo ele, seu nome não constava na lista de elite da prova, e, após tentar resolver a situação, foi informado que só poderia correr no pelotão geral.

Cirino estava inscrito para a prova de 21 km, mas realizou uma troca de inscrição com um amigo que correria os 42 km. Na largada, ele foi barrado por um membro da organização, que alegou que sua carteirinha da CBAt não estava válida, impedindo-o de competir.

Em nota oficial, a organização da Maratona de Pomerode esclareceu que Renato Cirino estava inscrito na prova de 21 km por meio de uma cortesia de patrocinador e que não houve solicitação para inclusão no pelotão de elite. A troca para os 42 km foi um procedimento realizado “indevidamente” por um integrante da equipe operacional, já que o prazo para alterações havia se encerrado. A direção técnica identificou o erro, comunicou o patrocinador de que a inscrição nos 42 km não seria válida, mas, mesmo assim, o atleta compareceu à largada com o número de peito da distância maior e foi informado que não poderia participar.

Etapas e ranking da ASICS Run Challenge

O circuito ASICS Run Challenge, com etapas de 4 km, 7 km e 15 km, já passou por Belo Horizonte, Brasília, Fortaleza, Salvador e Recife. A última etapa do ano será em Florianópolis, no dia 8 de novembro, e as inscrições ainda estão abertas. A organização criou um ranking “Top 50 Brasil” para os atletas que participaram das provas ao longo do ano. Para se inscrever na etapa de Florianópolis com desconto, utilize o cupom CORRIDANOAR10.

Resultados da Ultra BM

A Ultra BM aconteceu no último sábado sob forte chuva, o que deixou o percurso com muito lama e trechos alagados. Na prova de 75 km, o vencedor no masculino foi Paulo Adriano Campos dos Santos, com o tempo de 5h24min52s. No feminino, a vitória foi de Roselene Costa de Sousa, que completou a distância em 6h48min05s. Já na maratona de 42 km, o primeiro lugar masculino ficou com Thales A. M. Galindo (2h41min50s), e o feminino com Sandra Batista dos Santos (3h31min38s). A prova de 75 km teve 429 concluintes, o dobro dos 245 que finalizaram a maratona. Além disso, 309 equipes participaram do revezamento.
